newsitem.title: INDIA: Overvalued rupee seen hurting Indian exports.
newsitem.headline: Overvalued rupee seen hurting Indian exports.

text.p: An overvalued rupee is contributing to a slowdown in Indian exports, representatives of the country's export industries said on Thursday.
"The rupee is overvalued at a time when exporters' costs have been rising," N.K. Goyal, chairman of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations (FIEO), told Reuters.
FIEO represents export organisations from the textile, engineering, chemical, jewellery and other sectors that make up the bulk of Indian exports.

"Look at how the dollar has moved up against the mark and the yen in recent months," said Ramu Deora, chairman of the Chemicals, Pharmaceuticals and Cosmetics Export Promotion Council (Chemexcil), a constituent of FIEO.
"But the rupee continues at 35.88 (against the dollar)," Deora said.

After trading steady at 31.37 to a dollar for nearly two years, the Indian rupee started weakening in mid-1995. It touched a record low of 38.50 against the dollar in February 1996, but soon gained in value again to 34.0 in March.
The rupee has been stuck in the 35.88/89 range in recent weeks.
The independent Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE) said that during the current 1996/97 financial year (April-March), export performance deteriorated with each quarter.
Exports grew by 13 percent in the first quarter, 5.7 percent in the second quarter and one percent in the third quarter, it said in its January review of the economy.
"My exporters feel they could have done a lot better if the exchange rate was 38 rupees to a dollar," Deora said.

Indian exporters have been busy selling their export proceeds in the forward dollar market in recent weeks as they don't expect a sharp depreciation of the rupee in the near-term, foreign exchange dealers said.
"Exporters are selling at 38-plus for August (dollars payable in August 1997)," said a bank dealer in Bombay, adding that they are also selling dollars outright.
Analysts said the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) would not allow the rupee to depreciate faster because it would inflate India's oil import bill and lead to a worsening of the fiscal deficit.

"(Corporations) are waiting for the budget before reviewing their present strategy of hedging exports and keeping imports unhedged," said a dealer at a French bank in Bombay. Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram presents the national budget for fiscal 1997/98 on Friday.
Some dealers expect the RBI to intervene to effect a sharper depreciation of the rupee after the budget is passed by parliament.
"They (RBI) have been buying dollars almost daily last week," said a dealer. "They only have to raise their dollar buying rate for the rupee to depreciate," he said.
Analysts differ on whether the government would want a faster depreciation of the rupee. Some analysts believe the government has no choice as Indian exports are slowing down.
